itineraries.title: Netherlands Tour: Tulips, Windmills and Villages
itineraries.climate: Best time: mid-April to mid-May for tulips in bloom (Lisse, Keukenhof) and May–September for the rest, with temperatures of 15–23°C. Avoid November–March: cold, constant biting wind, frequent rain (2–8°C). Always bring a windbreaker, even in summer.

visits.text: Explore Schiermonnikoog, one of the inhabited West Frisian Islands. Declared a national park in 1989, this island offers unspoiled nature with its wild dunes, pine forests and exceptional tidal mudflats listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Discover the Wadden Sea, a unique ecosystem classified as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. This intertidal zone harbors remarkable biodiversity and constitutes one of the last great natural wetlands in Europe.

activities.text: Join a guided mudflat walk with expert local guides. At low tide, you'll explore this fascinating world populated by crabs, shellfish, and migratory birds—an unforgettable sensory experience.

Enjoy Europe's widest beach with its kilometer of fine sand stretching as far as the eye can see. This immense space where sky and sea blend together offers a sense of absolute freedom, far from any urbanization.

visits.text: Discover Hindeloopen, one of the eleven historic cities of Friesland, famous for its unique decorative art. This fishing village on the shores of the IJsselmeer has developed over the centuries a distinctive artistic style recognizable by its colorful floral motifs on dark backgrounds.

activities.text: Admire the traditional houses adorned with Frisian folk paintings in their characteristic hues. The local museum displays furniture and objects painted according to this craft tradition passed down from generation to generation.

Stroll along the small harbor where traditional sailboats sit alongside captains' houses. The peaceful atmosphere of this village with its narrow lanes invites contemplation and discovery of authentic Frisian heritage.

visits.text: Marvel at the largest tulip fields in the Netherlands in the Noordoostpolder. This region northeast of Amsterdam boasts over 2,000 hectares of cultivable land where tulips create natural tableaux of brilliant colors at every turn.

Visit the Noordoostpolder tulip information center to understand the fascinating history of 'Tulipmania' and the economic importance of this emblematic flower. Interactive exhibitions reveal the secrets of bulb cultivation and trade.

activities.text: Explore the colorful fields on foot, by bike, or by car as you please. Far from the crowds of Keukenhof, this region offers a more intimate and authentic experience amid the flower fields, with views of multicolored rows stretching as far as the eye can see.

visits.text: Discover Giethoorn, nicknamed the 'Venice of the North,' a fairytale village where streets are replaced by canals. This unique gem of the Netherlands consists of picturesque thatched cottages connected by over 180 wooden bridges, creating a storybook setting preserved for centuries.

activities.text: Travel by traditional boat through canals lined with flowering gardens and thatched-roof houses. The silence is broken only by birdsong and the lapping of water, offering an absolutely magical, timeless escape.

Explore the walking and cycling paths that wind between properties with manicured gardens. Each bridge you cross reveals a new perspective on this lakeside village where nature and human dwellings coexist in perfect harmony.

visits.text: Explore Elburg, a remarkably preserved medieval fortified town. This former Hanseatic city has retained its original rectangular layout with its ramparts, monumental gates, and maze of cobblestone streets that transport visitors several centuries back in time.

activities.text: Wander through the historic center where every building tells a story. The gabled facades, the old town hall, and St. Nicholas Church testify to the past prosperity of this merchant town that traded throughout the Baltic.

Walk along the restored ramparts offering panoramic views of the old town and surrounding polders. This walk along the fortifications allows you to appreciate medieval defensive engineering while admiring the typical Dutch landscape.

visits.text: Spend a magical day at Efteling, the largest theme park in the Netherlands and the fourth-largest in Europe. This legendary attraction in the province of Brabant has enchanted young and old for decades with its fairytale worlds and thrilling rides.

Immerse yourself in the famous Fairy Tale Forest where the stories of Little Red Riding Hood, Mother Holle, and Sleeping Beauty come to life. These enchanting displays, created with remarkable attention to detail, delight visitors of all ages.

activities.text: Take on the park's six roller coasters, from classic wooden ones to ultra-modern attractions. Thrill-seekers will find plenty to enjoy among the water rides and dark rides that have made Efteling famous.

Explore the different themed kingdoms of the park that combine tradition and innovation. Efteling has preserved its nostalgic charm while offering contemporary attractions, creating a unique experience in Europe.

visits.text: Admire the 19 historic windmills of Kinderdijk, listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1997. These 18th-century mills, built to pump water from the polders, form one of the most impressive and best-preserved groups of windmills in the Netherlands.

Visit the museum windmill to understand the ingenious workings of these hydraulic machines. These mills pump water into the “Nieuwen Waterschap,” which flows into the Lek River, allowing farmland to be maintained below sea level.

activities.text: Cycle along the paths that wind between the majestic windmills. In any season, these giants with their turning sails offer a fascinating spectacle, especially at sunset when their silhouettes stand out against the fiery sky.

Discover the history of the Dutch people's age-old struggle against water at this iconic site. These windmills bear witness to the ingenuity of a people who reclaimed land from the sea and kept it habitable for centuries.

visits.text: Explore Madurodam, The Hague's famous miniature park presenting the Netherlands at a scale of 1:25. From the Royal Palace to the Rijksmuseum, including Schiphol Airport and tulip fields, discover the country's iconic monuments down to the smallest detail.

Discover Scheveningen, the most popular seaside resort in the Netherlands welcoming up to 18 million visitors per year. Its 381-meter pier, lively beaches, and vibrant boulevard make it an unmissable destination on the Dutch coast.

activities.text: Take part in Madurodam's interactive activities: close a storm surge barrier, load containers at the Port of Rotterdam, or mix your own beats at the DJ console. This fun park lets you learn about Dutch history in an entertaining way.
Climb the observation tower at the end of Scheveningen pier for breathtaking panoramic views of the North Sea. The most adventurous can even bungee jump from this iconic structure.

visits.text: Visit Keukenhof, nicknamed the Garden of Europe and considered one of the most beautiful spring gardens in the world. With over seven million tulips, daffodils, and hyacinths in bloom, this 32-hectare park offers an absolutely spectacular explosion of colors from March to May.

Discover the fascinating history of the tulip and 17th-century “Tulipmania” through the park's exhibitions. This period when bulbs were worth more than houses reflects the Dutch passion for this flower that has become a national symbol.

activities.text: Admire the 50 sculptures by Dutch artists scattered throughout the park, making Keukenhof the largest sculpture park in the Netherlands. Contemporary art is in harmonious dialogue with the floral arrangements in a successful marriage of nature and culture.

Embark on an excursion by traditional wooden boat through the surrounding tulip fields. These old boats, once used by gardeners, offer a unique perspective on the multicolored rows stretching endlessly into the distance.

visits.text: Enjoy the award-winning beach of Bergen aan Zee, honored eight times with the Blue Flag for its exemplary cleanliness and safety. This seaside resort founded specifically as a holiday destination attracts thousands of visitors each year seeking pristine nature and fresh North Sea air.

activities.text: Try your hand at water sports on this coast renowned for its ideal conditions. Kitesurfing and sailing are practiced here in an exceptional setting, with schools offering lessons for all levels, from beginners to experienced participants.

Stroll along the long stretch of fine sand where the North Sea laps at the shore. The infinite horizon and preserved dunes create a soothing landscape, perfect for long invigorating walks to the sound of the waves.

map_keywords: Royal Netherlands Navy Museum Den Helder

visits.text: Visit the Royal Netherlands Navy Museum, housed in the former naval base of Den Helder. This institution traces the glorious maritime history of the Netherlands, a nation of navigators and explorers that dominated the seas for centuries.
Explore the town center of Den Helder with its elegant red brick buildings typical of Dutch architecture. This strategic port city offers a fascinating blend of military history and provincial charm.

activities.text: Explore the surrounding tulip fields on an outing on foot, by bicycle or by car. From mid-April to mid-May, the region bursts into spectacular colour, with a sea of flowers alongside the actual sea in a striking natural scene.
Pick your own tulips at the Floratuin garden, which offers over 100 different varieties. This unique experience allows you to create your personalized bouquet from a dazzling palette of colors.

visits.text: Visit Alkmaar's famous cheese market on the Waagplein, an uninterrupted tradition since 1622. Every Friday morning from late March to late September, cheese carriers dressed in white transport the cheese wheels on wooden carrying frames according to age-old rituals.

Discover the Alkmaar Cheese Museum, which traces the fascinating history of Dutch cheese production. Through traditional tools, period paintings, and interactive demonstrations, you'll understand why Dutch cheese is renowned worldwide.

activities.text: Explore Alkmaar's historic center with its typical brick buildings and charming canals. This medieval town is full of architectural treasures and offers an authentically Dutch atmosphere far from the tourist crowds of the major cities.

visits.text: Explore Volendam, one of the most iconic fishing villages in the Netherlands. This traditional port on the shores of the IJsselmeer has preserved its old-world charm with its cobblestone lanes, wooden houses, and residents who still sometimes wear traditional costume during local festivals.

activities.text: Stroll along the picturesque harbor where colorful fishing boats gently bob. Admire the typical facades of fishermen's houses and soak up the authentic maritime atmosphere of this village that has inspired numerous artists for centuries.

map_keywords: Colored wooden houses Broek in Waterland

visits.text: Discover Broek in Waterland, a picturesque village of colorful wooden houses that seems frozen in time. This authentic 17th-century gem, located just a few kilometers from Amsterdam, offers total immersion in traditional Holland with its peaceful canals and bucolic atmosphere untouched by mass tourism.

activities.text: Wander along the canals lined with historic houses featuring pastel facades and admire the typically Dutch architecture of this heritage-listed village. The reflections of old houses in the calm water create a postcard-perfect setting ideal for photography enthusiasts.

seo.h1_title: Netherlands Tour: Tulips, Windmills and Villages
seo.intro_paragraph: Embark on a journey through the hidden treasures of the Netherlands, where multicolored tulip fields alternate with majestic windmills and picturesque canal villages. This 12 days itinerary takes you far from the tourist crowds to discover an authentic Holland of centuries-old traditions, breathtaking landscapes, and a cultural heritage unique in the world.
seo.seo_hook: A 12-day tour of the Netherlands: tulips as far as the eye can see, Kinderdijk's UNESCO-listed windmills, Giethoorn, the Venice of the North, and authentic villages.
featured_list: The 19 historic windmills of Kinderdijk, UNESCO World Heritage Site
Giethoorn, the magical Venice of the North with no roads

The pristine island of Schiermonnikoog and the Wadden Sea

itineraries.title: Southern Netherlands Road Trip: Tulips, Windmills, the Delta and Cities of Art
itineraries.subtitle: From The Hague to Haarlem via Maastricht and Keukenhof—9 days exploring the best of the southern Netherlands
itineraries.notes: Keukenhof is only open from mid-March to mid-May - plan accordingly. The Maastricht detour (D7) can be skipped to shorten the trip to 8 days.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: mid-April to early May for tulip fields in bloom, with temperatures of 10 to 18°C. Avoid November-February (frequent rain, icy winds, no flowers in bloom). The country is windy all year round, so bring a windbreaker even in spring.

visits.text: The Mauritshuis occupies a 1644 mansion on the edge of the Hofvijver, built for Count Johan Maurits van Nassau. You'll see Vermeer's Girl with a Pearl Earring, Rembrandt's The Anatomy Lesson of Dr. Nicolaes Tulp, and Fabritius's The Goldfinch. Allow 1 hour and 30 minutes: the museum is compact but every room is a masterpiece. Beat the crowds by arriving after 3pm or on Thursday evenings.

The Binnenhof is a parliamentary complex whose origins date back to the 13th century under Count Floris IV. The Ridderzaal, the Knights' Hall with its 18 m wooden beams, is part of this historic ensemble. The inner courtyard and the Ridderzaal are currently closed for renovation. To discover the site, walk along the edge of the Hofvijver: you can view the façades of the parliamentary complex from outside and see their reflections in the water.

Madurodam recreates the Netherlands at 1:25 scale: Kinderdijk windmills, Schiphol Airport, Rotterdam harbor, the Royal Palace. It's the perfect place to grasp the country's geography before experiencing it in real life. Allow an hour - it's fun for all ages.

Scheveningen is The Hague's seaside resort, 5 km from the city center. Its pier extends 380 meters over the North Sea, and its fine-sand beach stretches 11 km. Perfect for a late afternoon break before watching the sun descend over the water.

activities.text: A stroll along Scheveningen's seafront at sunset—the Dutch bike here from downtown along the Het Haagse Beek canal. The view of the North Sea, often accompanied by strong winds, immediately sets the tone for the Netherlands.

visits.text: Explore Delft's historic center on foot, between the canals and the Markt. The Nieuwe Kerk houses the tomb of William of Orange, founder of the Dutch Republic, and its bell tower offers a view across the whole city. Next door, the Renaissance town hall dates from 1618.

Royal Delft—the Koninklijke Porceleyne Fles—was founded in 1653 and remains the only one of the original 32 Delftware factories still in operation. You'll watch artisans hand-paint blue and white patterns using cobalt oxide, whose blue color only appears after firing at 1,200°C. The visit lasts 1 hour and 30 minutes, and you can observe painters at work in the studio.

The Vermeer Centrum traces the life of the painter born in Delft in 1632. None of his 36 paintings are displayed here, but high-definition reproductions allow you to study his use of light up close. It provides the best context for understanding what you saw at the Mauritshuis the day before.

activities.text: Rent a bike and meander along Delft's canals—the city is flat, and bike paths wind around the bridges and alleyways of the medieval center. In an hour's ride, you'll pass through neighborhoods most visitors never see.

visits.text: Kinderdijk's 19 windmills were built between 1738 and 1740 to drain the Alblasserwaard polders - a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1997. You can enter two museum windmills and take the sightseeing boat included in the ticket. Arrive before 10 a.m. to avoid groups, or take the Waterbus from Rotterdam for an approach along the river. Plan a round trip from Rotterdam for this visit.

Piet Blom's Cube Houses (Kubuswoningen) were built in 1984 in Rotterdam: 38 cubes tilted 45° above the Blaak bridge vaults. You can visit one of them, the Kijk-Kubus, to understand how people live inside an impossible angle.

The Markthal is an arch 40 meters high and 120 meters long, inaugurated in 2014 and designed by the architecture firm MVRDV. Its interior vault is entirely covered with an 11,000 m² digital mural depicting a cornucopia—fruits, vegetables, giant insects. Stop here for lunch: around a hundred stalls occupy the ground floor.

Delfshaven is a historic district of Rotterdam that survived the bombing of May 1940. It was from here that the Pilgrim Fathers departed on July 22, 1620, aboard the Speedwell before joining the Mayflower in England. The 15th-century Pilgrim Fathers Church still stands facing the canals.

activities.text: Bike ride through Rotterdam along the Erasmus Bridge and waterfront - the city was rebuilt from scratch after the German bombings of May 1940, and you'll discover architecture unique in Europe, blending brutalism, high-tech, and urban experimentation.

visits.text: The Oosterscheldekering is the largest structure in the Delta Works - 9 km long between the islands of Schouwen-Duiveland and Noord-Beveland, with 62 steel gates that automatically close whenever the sea rises more than 3 meters above Amsterdam's reference level. This storm surge barrier was inaugurated in 1986 by Queen Beatrix. You can drive across it on the N57.

Neeltje Jans is the artificial island built to assemble the barrier's 65 concrete pillars. Now converted into an information center, it presents the Delta Experience - an exhibition about the catastrophic floods of 1953, which killed 1 835 people and forced the evacuation of 70 000, prompting the entire Delta Works project. The site is around 21 km from Middelburg, a 20-minute drive.

Middelburg is the capital of Zeeland and one of the VOC cities - the Dutch East India Company had its regional headquarters here in the 17th century. The 15th-century Gothic town hall borders the Markt. Don't miss the Lange Jan tower of the 12th-century abbey, visible for kilometers around.

Veere is a fortified village on the shores of Veerse Meer, frozen in its medieval setting. Its grand 15th-century houses on the quay belonged to Scottish wool merchants who held a monopoly on the wool trade with the Netherlands. Today it's a vacation destination for recreational boaters.

activities.text: Walk along the beaches and dunes of the Zeeland coast - Domburg or Westkapelle offer wild dune landscapes opening onto the North Sea. Zeeland has one of the country's windiest and most pristine coastlines.

visits.text: Sint-Janskathedraal is the pinnacle of Brabantine Gothic architecture in the Netherlands. Built between 1380 and 1530, it rises 73 meters high and stretches 115 meters long. Look closely at its 96 sculpted figures on the flying buttresses - dragons, angels, and fantastical creatures unique in the country. Admission is free; guided tower tours offer panoramic views.

The Jheronimus Bosch Art Center occupies a former church and presents high-definition reproductions of the complete works of Jheronimus Bosch, born here around 1450. You won't travel to Madrid to see the original Garden of Earthly Delights, but here you'll study it centimeter by centimeter through enlargements.

The Binnendieze is a network of partly underground canals that once extended 22 km beneath the streets of 's-Hertogenbosch. Board an electric boat and glide under houses, town halls, and historic cellars - a unique way to see a medieval city from below. The guided tour lasts about 50 minutes.

activities.text: Grab a bossche bol from one of the downtown bakers—this giant pastry filled with whipped cream and coated in dark chocolate has been the quintessential specialty of 's-Hertogenbosch for centuries. Don't miss the buzz of the market square in late afternoon either.

visits.text: The Van Abbemuseum is one of the Netherlands' most important modern and contemporary art museums. Its collection includes works by Picasso, Chagall, Mondrian, and El Lissitzky. The 2003 architectural extension creates a dialogue between the original 1936 brick building and a spectacular contemporary volume.

Strijp-S is the former 27-hectare Philips industrial complex, closed to the public for decades - nicknamed the 'Forbidden City.' Now converted into a creative district, it houses lofts in the Anton and Gerard factories, artist studios, galleries, and cafés in the former manufacturing workshops. This is where Dutch Design Week takes place every October.

The Philips Museum traces the history of the industrial empire founded in Eindhoven in 1891 by Gerard Philips—from the first electric light bulb to the razor, by way of radio and television. The interactive presentation is accessible to visitors of all ages.

activities.text: Wander through Strijp-S in the evening—street art covers the old industrial buildings, outdoor seating fills the interior courtyards, and local designer boutiques stay open late. It's the best place to understand how Eindhoven reinvented itself as a design capital after Philips left.

visits.text: Sint-Servaasbasiliek is considered the oldest church in the Netherlands, built over the tomb of Saint Servatius, Bishop of Tongeren who died in 384. The current Romanesque nave dates from the 11th century. In the treasury room, don't miss Saint Servatius's 1160 reliquary shrine, a masterpiece of Mosan goldwork in gilded copper and precious stones.

Boekhandel Dominicanen is a 13th-century Gothic church converted into a bookstore in 2006. A three-level steel structure was inserted into the nave for bookshelves, and a café occupies the former chancel. The international press voted it the world's most beautiful bookstore—and you'll understand why the moment you walk through the door.

The Vrijthof is Maastricht's main square, bordered by the Sint-Servaasbasiliek. The terraces stretch for more than 200 meters facing the Baroque façades: it is one of the most beautiful public spaces in the Netherlands.

Sint Pietersberg is a limestone hill south of Maastricht that's been quarried since Roman times - its tunnel network exceeds 200 km. Guided tours reveal historic inscriptions, wall paintings, and the location of a vault carved in 1944 to protect Rembrandt's Night Watch. Bring warm clothing: it's 9°C year-round.

activities.text: Stroll along the Meuse River and through the Wyck district - across the medieval Sint Servaasbrug, this historic neighborhood houses independent boutiques, galleries, and restaurants. The bridge itself is one of the oldest in the country.

visits.text: Keukenhof is the world's largest flower garden: 32 hectares, 7 million bulbs, and over 800 tulip varieties. In 2026 it's open from March 19 to May 10 - peak bloom falls between April 10 and 30. Arrive at opening time (8am) to photograph the paths without crowds.

The Bollenstreek fields stretch between Lisse, Hillegom, and Noordwijk: solid-color bands of several hectares each - red, yellow, purple, white - that growers cultivate for bulb sales. This spectacle is visible from roads or bike paths. Note: flowers are usually cut in late April to strengthen the bulbs.

activities.text: Rent a bike and follow the Tulip Bike Tour - a signposted route of 10 or 25 km through the Bollenstreek fields, entirely free of charge. The route runs alongside working farms, passes Keukenhof Castle and allows for photo stops. You can rent a bike at Keukenhof's P1 parking lot or in the center of Lisse.

visits.text: Haarlem's Grote Markt is one of the Netherlands' most beautiful squares, dominated by Sint-Bavokerk - a 1370 Gothic church rising 78 meters high. The 1738 Christian Müller organ was played by a 10-year-old Mozart during his 1766 visit, and also by Handel. Admission is free.

The Frans Hals Museum occupies the Oudemannenhuis, an almshouse for elderly men founded in 1609 - and it was Frans Hals himself who painted the 1664 portraits of the regents of this establishment. The collection brings together more than twelve original paintings by the master along with works by his Haarlem contemporaries like Judith Leyster and Jacob van Ruisdael.

The Teylers Museum is the oldest museum in the Netherlands, continuously open to the public since 1784. Its founder, banker Pieter Teyler van der Hulst, bequeathed his fortune in 1778 to create a place dedicated to science and the arts. You'll see drawings by Michelangelo and Raphael, giant fossils, and 18th-century scientific instruments in their original neoclassical setting.

activities.text: Stroll through Haarlem's pedestrian streets and hofjes - these hidden courtyards surrounded by small houses, founded as early as the 14th century, are a little-known treasure. The Hofje de Bakenesserkamer (1395) is the oldest in the country. Haarlem is connected by train to Amsterdam Schiphol: it is a city of art without the crowds.

seo.h1_title: Southern Netherlands Road Trip: Tulips, Windmills, the Delta and Cities of Art
seo.intro_paragraph: This 9-day circuit takes you through the best of the southern Netherlands, from The Hague to Haarlem via Rotterdam, Zeeland, and Maastricht. You'll discover exceptional museums like the Mauritshuis and its Vermeer masterpieces, the spectacular engineering of the Delta Works, Kinderdijk's 19 UNESCO windmills, and the tulip fields of the Bollenstreek. An authentic and varied Holland, far from Amsterdam's crowds.
seo.seo_hook: From Girl with a Pearl Earring to Keukenhof's tulips: 9 days exploring UNESCO windmills, the Delta Works, and cities of art in the southern Netherlands.

itineraries.title: Northern Netherlands Road Trip: Amsterdam, Friesland, Wadden Islands & Giethoorn
itineraries.subtitle: From Golden Age canals to the wild islands of the Wadden Sea, via the green Venice of Overijssel
itineraries.notes: A road trip beyond Amsterdam to reveal the Netherlands that most travelers never see: Friesland with its own language, the island of Texel and its seals, Giethoorn and Schokland - a former island forcibly evacuated in the face of the sea, now surrounded by fields.
itineraries.climate: Best time: May–June and September, temperatures of 15–22 °C, maximum sunshine. Avoid November–March (cold, damp, gray weather and icy winds on Texel). Rain is possible year-round; bring a windbreaker.

visits.text: Amsterdam's Canal Ring (Grachtengordel) has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2010: three concentric canals dug in the 17th century, lined with 1,500 gabled houses. Stroll along the Herengracht, the most elegant, to understand why Amsterdam was the world's commercial capital during the VOC era.

The Jordaan was a working-class neighborhood in the 17th century—today it's Amsterdam's most sought-after district. Its narrow lanes, flower-draped bridges, and quintessentially Dutch brown cafés deserve an hour of aimless wandering.

The Rijksmuseum houses over 8,000 objects spanning 800 years of Dutch history, including Rembrandt's The Night Watch (3.6 m × 4.4 m) and Vermeer's The Milkmaid. The neo-Gothic building was designed by Pierre Cuypers and opened in 1885. Book your ticket online: time slots fill up fast.

activities.text: A canal cruise departing from Centraal Station is the best way to grasp Amsterdam's 17th-century fan-shaped urban plan. From the deck, you'll see the leaning houses and the city's 1,500 bridges from an angle impossible to capture on foot. Allow 1 hour and 15 minutes.

Rent a bike and pedal through the Jordaan to the Brouwersgracht—considered Amsterdam's most photogenic canal. Early morning, before 9 a.m., it's almost deserted. Bikes can be rented everywhere near Centraal in minutes.

visits.text: Zaanse Schans is a living museum village 20 minutes north of Amsterdam, where green wooden houses and 17th- and 18th-century windmills have been gathered since 1961. Entry to the village is free—only the windmills and certain workshops charge admission. Arrive on a weekday before 10 a.m. to experience the atmosphere without the crowds.

You can visit several working windmills: De Kat produces pigments for dyes, De Zoeker has pressed oil since 1610, and Het Jonge Schaap is a sawmill. Climb onto a windmill's gallery for the best view over the Zaan River.

The Negen Straatjes (Nine Streets) form a grid of lanes perpendicular to the canals in the Jordaan. Vintage boutiques, concept stores, and independent cafés share these nine little streets: this is where Amsterdammers do their shopping.

activities.text: The workshops at Zaanse Schans offer continuous demonstrations: wooden clog making (you'll see the carving machine in action), artisanal cheese-making with tastings, and traditional baking. Plan on an hour to visit several.

visits.text: Alkmaar's cheese market (Kaasmarkt) takes place every Friday morning, from the last Friday in March to the last Friday in September, from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. on the Waagplein. The cheese carriers' guild has existed since 1593: you will see carts loaded with wheels of Gouda, ritualized negotiations and the weighing at the Waag. It is the oldest and most famous cheese market in the Netherlands.
The Hollands Kaasmuseum is housed in Alkmaar's former Waag (weigh house), a 14th-century building. It traces the history of the cheese trade in the region from the Middle Ages to the present day.

Alkmaar's historic center can be explored on foot along its canals: gabled houses, pedestrian streets, and the atmosphere of a well-preserved small provincial Dutch town. Allow 45 minutes for a complete circuit.

activities.text: Rent a bike and cycle through Zuid-Kennemerland National Park: wooded dunes, semi-wild Konik horses and trails toward Bloemendaal beach. Allow for a day trip from Alkmaar.

visits.text: Texel is the largest of the five Dutch Wadden Sea islands, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2009. Its 30 km of North Sea beach, dunes, and nature reserves cover more than a quarter of the island. It's also the most accessible—just 20 minutes by ferry from Den Helder.

Ecomare is a seal rescue center, marine aquarium, and nature museum dedicated to the Wadden Sea and the North Sea. You'll see harbor seals and gray seals in rehabilitation before their release. Allow 1 hour and 15 minutes for the complete visit.

The Texel Lighthouse (Vuurtoren Eierland) has stood at the island's northern tip since 1864. Its brick-red exterior makes it recognizable from afar. Climb it for a view over the tidal currents of the Wadden Sea and the exposed sandbanks.

activities.text: Take the Den Helder → Texel ferry (20 min, cars accepted), then rent a bike just outside the terminal: the island has 140 km of marked, flat cycling paths. Head for De Slufter, the only area in the Netherlands where the North Sea flows freely into the dunes, forming unique salt marshes.

visits.text: The Oldehove is Leeuwarden's leaning tower: begun in 1529, construction was halted because it was already tilting before completion. The result leans more than the Tower of Pisa. Climb it for an off-kilter view over the rooftops of the Frisian capital.

The Fries Museum tells the story of Friesland, a Dutch province with its own official language—Frisian, spoken by 400,000 people. The contemporary building overlooks Wilhelminaplein and its collections cover art, archaeology, and regional culture.

Central Leeuwarden can be explored on foot along the canals: the city was European Capital of Culture in 2018. Its 17th-century patrician houses and cafés lining the canals deserve an hour of wandering.

activities.text: Take an excursion to Franeker (about 21 km from Leeuwarden, a 20-minute drive) to visit the Eise Eisinga planetarium: the world's oldest working planetarium, built between 1774 and 1781 by a wool carder on his living room ceiling. Inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2023, it still shows the actual positions of the planets today thanks to 10,000 hand-forged nails.

visits.text: In Giethoorn, you travel by electric boat between thatched farmhouses connected by wooden bridges. The village has around fifty bridges for barely 2,800 inhabitants. Head out to explore before 10 a.m.: afterward, the canals fill with fluisterboten.

Museum Giethoorn is housed in a former thatched-roof farmhouse. It traces the life of the peat diggers who carved out the canals in the Middle Ages by extracting peat—it was precisely this extraction that created the village's network of waterways.

activities.text: Rent a silent electric boat in Giethoorn and glide between thatched-roof farms for two hours. No license required; rental operators give you brief instructions before departure. Tip: bring a cooler and picnic on the water.

Weerribben-Wieden National Park, surrounding Giethoorn, is northwestern Europe's largest peat marsh. Take a bike or continue by boat to venture into the reeds, lakes, and silent canals. Reed buntings and corncrakes nest here.

visits.text: Schokland is the first Dutch site inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List (1995). This former Zuiderzee island was forcibly evacuated in 1859 because the flooding could not be contained. Since the polder was drained in 1942, it floats amid farmland like an anachronistic relic. More than 160 archaeological sites have been identified here, including 4,000-year-old human footprints.

Urk is a fishing village that was still an island in 1942 before the Noordoostpolder was drained. Its inhabitants still say they live “on Urk” rather than “in Urk.” Stroll through the winding alleyways down to the active fishing harbor, one of the Netherlands' most important.

Urk's museum traces how the draining of the Zuiderzee transformed an isolated island into a polder village connected to the mainland. Photographs, fishing objects, and reconstructions illustrate life before and after 1942.

activities.text: The walk along Urk's dike facing the IJsselmeer offers one of the Netherlands' most singular views: an endless lake horizon where the Zuiderzee sea once lay. Fishing boats return in late afternoon—the best time to see the harbor in action.

visits.text: Utrecht's Domtoren rises to 112.5 meters—it's the tallest church tower in the Netherlands. Built between 1321 and 1382, it became separated from the cathedral after the nave collapsed during a storm in 1674. Climb the 465 steps: on clear days, you can glimpse Amsterdam.

The Oudegracht is Utrecht's main canal, dug in the Middle Ages along the former Rhine riverbed. Its unique feature, found nowhere else in the world: low quays on two levels (werfkelders), medieval cellars converted into café and restaurant terraces right beside the water.

Museum Speelklok is housed in a 14th-century medieval church and contains the Netherlands' largest collection of self-playing musical instruments: music boxes, barrel organs, giant carillons, and mechanical orchestras. The instruments are played during free guided tours every hour.

activities.text: Follow the walking loop along the Oudegracht, Nieuwegracht, and Lepelenburg Park: an easy 4 km, taking about 1 hour and 30 minutes to discover Utrecht at water level, beneath bridges and alongside terraces. It's the best way to understand the two-level canal architecture.

visits.text: The Van Gogh Museum holds the world's largest collection of the artist's works: over 200 paintings, 500 drawings, and 700 letters. Don't miss Sunflowers, The Bedroom, and The Potato Eaters. Booking online is essential—tickets often sell out two weeks in advance.

Vondelpark is Amsterdam's green lung: 47 hectares of lawns, ponds, and outdoor stages five minutes from the Museum Quarter. In summer, free concerts take place in the evenings. It's the perfect spot to catch your breath between museums.

Amsterdam-Noord is reached by free ferry from behind Centraal Station; take the one that serves NDSM. The former NDSM shipyard is home to bars, artists' studios and monumental street art. A side of Amsterdam that tourists in a hurry never see.

activities.text: The Waterlooplein flea market is open every day except Sunday, and the Albert Cuyp Market, open since 1905, is the Netherlands' largest street market. Both are less than 20 minutes' walk from the Rijksmuseum—choose one to conclude your stay.

seo.h1_title: Northern Netherlands Road Trip: Amsterdam, Friesland, Wadden Islands & Giethoorn
seo.intro_paragraph: From Amsterdam's UNESCO-listed Baroque canals to the wild dunes of the island of Texel, this 9-day road trip crosses a country that reclaimed its land from the sea. You will glide quietly through Giethoorn, discover the working windmills of Zaanse Schans and stop at Schokland - the first Dutch island inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List, now surrounded by polder fields.
seo.seo_hook: 9 days traversing the northern Netherlands, from Amsterdam's baroque canals to Texel's wild dunes—via the green Venice of Giethoorn.
featured_list: Amsterdam: 17th-century UNESCO canals and Golden Age masters
Texel: the largest Wadden island, with seals and wild dunes
Giethoorn: the green Venice and its canals
Utrecht: the 112-meter Domtoren and medieval quays below street level

itineraries.title: Eastern Netherlands - Hanseatic League, Veluwe and Achterhoek in 10 Days
itineraries.subtitle: Ten days of Hanseatic towns, hidden castles and the best Van Gogh outside Amsterdam.
itineraries.notes: The region is ideal from May to September; Achterhoek castles have reduced hours off-season, check before you go. Get the Museumkaart: it covers the Kröller-Müller, the Openluchtmuseum and many other stops.
itineraries.climate: Best time: May–September, temperatures of 15–23°C, optimal sunshine for Giethoorn and the Veluwe park. Avoid November–March (grey, cold and damp, 2–8°C, frequent rain). Always pack a raincoat—showers are possible even in summer.

visits.text: Built in 1409, two years after Zwolle joined the Hanseatic League, the Sassenpoort is the sole surviving city gate from the old ramparts. Its 101,000 trachyte and sandstone blocks bear witness to the commercial wealth of the era. It's open Wednesdays and Saturdays from 11 AM to 5 PM, entrance €3, and features a permanent Hanseatic hall accessed via the medieval staircase.

Touristy but well done: Zwolle's Grote Markt is ringed by 16th-century merchant façades and a café terrace tucked into the Wijndragerstoren tower. A stone's throw away, Sint-Michaelskerk displays a statue of the archangel on its roof—there's a green version in the square, look for it. Saturday's open-air market remains one of the liveliest in Overijssel.

The scent of old paper and waxed wood greets you at Van der Velde in de Broeren, a bookshop housed since 2013 in a neo-Gothic church dating from 1901. The shelves climb all the way to the vaults, and a café occupies the chancel. An hour easily slips away. Avoid Sunday mornings, when it gets crowded.

activities.text: Take the trail around the star-shaped ramparts surrounding the historic centre: the outline of the old fortifications is still visible in the canal layout. The 2.4-km walk, signposted by the tourist office, passes beneath the Sassenpoort and alongside several towers still standing.

practical_info.tip: The route is flat and entirely bikeable; rent a bicycle at the station on arrival.

activities.text: If the sun cooperates, climb the 236 steps of the Peperbus to the first landing at 51 metres: the tower of the Onze-Lieve-Vrouwebasiliek soars to 75 metres but public access stops there, and the view over the polders and the IJssel is already clear. Check opening hours at the basilica before coming.

practical_info.tip: The climb is limited to certain days and time slots; check the basilica website beforehand.

visits.text: Unbearably touristy on July weekends, but virtually deserted at 8 AM: that's when Giethoorn reveals its true face. Founded in the 13th century, this village in Overijssel province is structured around 90 km of canals and 180 wooden bridges connecting peat islets. The thatched-roof farms — some dating from the 17th and 18th centuries — have no road in front of their doors. Mail is delivered by boat.

The splash of an oar replaces the car horn in Giethoorn, an officially car-free village integrated into Weerribben-Wieden National Park. The reed beds lining the canals are harvested each year using traditional methods to maintain biodiversity. The park covers a vast protected wetland north of the village, ideal for observing waterfowl at dawn.

activities.text: Rent an electric whisperboat as soon as you arrive — rental companies open early and the first hours are the quietest. Count on an hour and a half for the main circuit of inner canals. Electric boats are encouraged to protect the banks and wildlife. Avoid high-season weekends: the narrow canals can be gridlocked.

practical_info.tip: Reserve your whisperboat online the day before in summer; stock is limited.

visits.text: Kampen's own residents call their town an “open-air museum”. It's not an exaggeration: with nearly 500 monuments in its historic centre alone, Kampen packs more heritage per square metre than many provincial capitals. The square around the golden bridge—adorned with gold wheels since the Middle Ages—and the IJssel quays form a harmonious whole that is still full of life.

Built in the 14th century, the Bovenkerk, or Sint-Nicolaaskerk, dominates the IJssel waterfront with its Gothic nave. It houses an impressive organ and stained glass worth lingering over. A few steps away, the Koornmarktspoort is the town's oldest medieval gate — you can climb it for a panorama over the river. Kampen was also the first Dutch town to produce its own cigars: the De Eenhoorn factory still offers tours.

activities.text: The IJssel waterfront stretches for several hundred metres under the setting sun. Walk the quays up to the town bridge to see the golden wheels that have adorned its pylons since the Middle Ages. The waterside terraces come alive in the evening; the Proeflokaal De Stomme van Campen, with a view over the IJssel, serves local beers.

practical_info.tip: The IJssel waterfront is less than 5 minutes on foot from the centre.

visits.text: A perfect square, and it's real: Elburg's fortified town measures 250 by 415 metres, laid out in 1392 by Duke William I of Guelders to protect his Hanseatic town. The grid plan is flawless—only one street remains curved, the Krommesteeg, because of the terrain. Parking is outside the walls, a two-minute walk away. In summer, crowds can be heavy: arrive before 10 am.

The Vischpoort is the only gate still standing since 1592, when an opening was made in the old defensive tower to let fishing boats pass. On the town side it has windows; on the sea side it has none—its windowless face once served as an oil-lit lighthouse for fishermen. Museum Elburg is housed in the former 15th-century Agnietenklooster, with free entry to the courtyard.

activities.text: The green ramparts are a surprise: the Groene Wallen Wandeling follows the 16th-century fortifications from the outside, between moats and meadows. The complete circuit is less than 2 km. Along the way, spot the Deetman ropewalk, the oldest working rope-making facility in the Netherlands, visible from the Noorderwal.

practical_info.tip: The kazemattes (casemates) are open afternoons in summer; check local hours.

visits.text: Fairy-tale pages hanging on brick walls: the Anton Pieck Museum set up shop in this small Hanseatic town in 1984 on purpose — its medieval streets look exactly like the scenes the artist drew. The museum, opened by Pieck himself at age 89, reconstructs his original studio in the basement with his 1,500-kg engraving press. Adult entry around €12.50.

Born in 1895 in Den Helder, Anton Pieck designed the Sprookjesbos at Efteling and illustrated dozens of books and calendars recognisable throughout the Netherlands. A drawing teacher for forty years, he stayed true to his romantic style in the face of every modernist movement. The artistic school of the time saw it as mere nostalgia; his prints still sell in their thousands today.

activities.text: If you appreciate old organs, the route between the museum and the De Fortuin windmill passes through the Dijkpoort, one of Hattem's two medieval gates. The 1742 mill is sometimes in operation at weekends. The small town can be explored entirely on foot in under an hour; the views over the IJssel from higher ground are among the most unobstructed in the region.

practical_info.tip: De Fortuin windmill is open certain Saturdays in season; check before you go.

visits.text: Built between 1684 and 1686, Paleis Het Loo was the residence of the House of Orange-Nassau until 1962 before becoming a national museum. It reopened in 2023 after major renovations, and entry is now via an underground passage beneath a glass roof that lets the light through. The Baroque gardens, designed according to the vision of William III and Mary II, have been restored to their original state. Closed Mondays; adult ticket around €21.

The Baroque gardens are impeccable: they were designed by Claude Desgots, Le Nôtre's nephew, to impress royal visitors. Symmetrical parterres, fountains and sculpted hedges recreate the 17th-century state. In spring, the flowering is particularly spectacular. Allow at least an hour just for the gardens.

activities.text: Stop by the royal stables to see the exhibition of carriages and ceremonial vehicles. The space is less visited than the palace apartments and offers a striking contrast between the splendour of 18th-century coaches and the royal family's first automobiles. Count on 30 to 40 minutes.

practical_info.tip: The combined ticket for palace + stables + gardens is the most complete option.

visits.text: A museum lost in the forest, yet this is where the Van Goghs are — not Amsterdam. The Kröller-Müller Museum, opened in 1938 in the heart of De Hoge Veluwe National Park, houses the world's second-largest Van Gogh collection, with nearly 90 paintings and more than 180 drawings. Access requires a combined park + museum ticket; buy it online to avoid weekend queues.

Ninety Van Gogh paintings, and the silence between them. The Kröller-Müller sculpture garden covers 25 hectares of forest dotted with works by Rodin, Moore and other 20th-century artists. The walk from the car park takes twenty minutes; there are no constraints, and it's the largest sculpture garden in the Netherlands.

Jachthuis Sint Hubertus is a total work of art: this hunting lodge by architect H.P. Berlage, the former residence of the Kröller-Müllers, is one of the most important Dutch monuments. Access is only by guided tour, which must be booked online. It's located 3 km from the museum in the park, accessible on foot or by bike.

activities.text: Take a free white bicycle at the Otterlo entrance - the park provides 1,800 of them at its three entrances. This is a way to move freely around the 5,500 hectares of heathland, woodland and dunes in De Hoge Veluwe. Deer and wild boar are easy to spot in the morning on the open heathland.

practical_info.tip: White bikes are free but limited on public holidays; arrive early.

activities.text: If you love contemporary sculpture, the Kröller-Müller's 25-hectare garden deserves a visit in its own right, separate from the museum: the works reveal themselves around bends in the woodland paths, without signs. The Museonder, an underground museum about the park's wildlife, is well suited to children and takes less than an hour.

practical_info.tip: On weekdays after 2 PM, the museum is significantly less crowded according to the official site.

visits.text: The costumed actors at the Nederlands Openluchtmuseum truly inhabit their roles: brewer, blacksmith, tram driver. This 44-hectare open-air museum in Arnhem relocates authentic buildings from every region of the Netherlands and fills them with characters who talk about the past in the present tense. Allow a full day. The Museum Pass is accepted.

Arnhem deserves better than its reputation as the “city of the bridge too far”. Its Sonsbeek Park, right in the centre, hosts contemporary sculptures scattered across terraced lawns overlooking the town. The park is entirely free and little visited by foreign tourists—a real breath of fresh air.

In Sonsbeek Park, sculptures emerge from the morning mist among old beeches. The park dates from the 19th century and its landscape design makes it one of Gelderland's finest urban parks. It connects the Openluchtmuseum to Arnhem's city centre on foot in a pleasant hour's walk.

activities.text: If you visit on a weekday, the Openluchtmuseum is much less crowded than on weekends: the actors have more time for visitors and the interactive workshops are less busy. Allow at least three hours to see the brewery, windmill, farm and historic tram sections. The tram makes a circuit of the site.

practical_info.tip: Openluchtmuseum parking is paid; neighbouring Burgers' Zoo has shared parking.

activities.text: At the John Frost Bridge, a plaque commemorates the battle of September 1944. Walking across takes ten minutes, and the view of the Arnhem skyline is the best in the city. The Airborne Museum at Hartenstein, in Oosterbeek, is the leading museum on Operation Market Garden if you want to learn more.

practical_info.tip: The bridge is freely accessible at all hours.

visits.text: Kasteel Huis Bergh dates back to the 13th century — archives mention the site as early as 1227 — and ranks among the largest medieval castles in the Netherlands. Surrounded by moats, it houses a collection of early Italian period paintings, medieval manuscripts and northern European works from the 16th century. The gardens and inner courtyard are freely accessible; the guided castle tour costs €8 per adult.

The chained manuscripts in Huis Bergh's armoury and the black torches of the keep are reminders that this tower has never been captured since it was built. The castle archive, whose oldest document dates from 1227, is one of the best preserved in Gelderland. An audio guide in several languages traces the history of the lords of Van den Bergh.

activities.text: Climb Huis Bergh's defensive tower to see the lands of Montferland spread out towards Germany, just a few kilometres away. The estate comprises around 500 hectares of forests and farmland surrounding the castle. Concerts and exhibitions are held regularly in season—check the programme before coming.

practical_info.tip: The tower is accessible during guided tours only; reduced hours off-season.

visits.text: Officially a city of 170 inhabitants: the sign says “stadsgrens”—city limits—after just a few dozen metres. Bronkhorst received its city rights in 1482 and has never grown beyond its medieval core since. Red-brick houses with decorated façades line three main streets; a complete walk takes under twenty minutes. It's the kind of place you want to see before the “Instagram spot” signs appear.

Bronkhorst's chapel dates from 1344 and was once the private chapel of the castle of the lords of Bronckhorst. All that remains of the castle is the Slotheuvel, a castle mound visible on the way out of the village. The chapel now serves as a cultural centre with occasional exhibitions. It's the only standing medieval monument in Bronkhorst; its bell tower is visible from every point in the village.

activities.text: Take the little cable ferry across the IJssel to Brummen — a few minutes' crossing, a few euros. It's one of the few ferry links still operating on this stretch of river. On the other side, a short walk leads to the first IJssel levees with a view of Bronkhorst from the water.

practical_info.tip: The ferry runs from late March to late October; reduced hours on weekdays.

visits.text: Eight castles along 34 km: it sounds too good to be true—yet that is the reality of the cycling loop around Vorden, signposted since 1913. Most are private residences closed to the public, which makes them all the more fascinating. Kasteel Vorden, visible from the main road, is open six days a week with a freely accessible audio guide.

Kasteel Hackfort: its underground passage dating from the 14th century is one of the few parts open to the public, two afternoons a week. The historic kitchen garden, dating back to around 1790, is a must-see for garden lovers. The brasserie in the coach house cooks with vegetables from the garden. The first mention of Hackfort in the archives dates from 1392.

activities.text: Rent a bike in the village for the Achtkastelenroute, marked with yellow hexagonal signs from Vorden market square. The 34 km on paved roads pass Hackfort, Den Bramel, De Wildenborch and five other castles. A guided version is offered Wednesdays and Saturdays in summer.

practical_info.tip: The route is entirely on paved roads; a town bike suffices.

visits.text: Carel Willink's surrealist canvases—camels in front of Versailles, landscapes with a nuclear power station—hanging in the 14th-century halls of Kasteel Ruurlo create a striking contrast. Museum MORE has displayed around thirty of his works in this monumental setting since 2017. Access to the castle rooms requires a museum ticket; the English landscape park and orangery are free.

Kasteel Ruurlo has housed Carel Willink's works since 2017. The initiative came from collector Hans Melchers, who wanted to offer this 20th-century realist painter a worthy showcase. The castle rooms date back to the 14th century and have been restored to combine several centuries of architecture. Together, they form one of Gelderland's most distinctive art museums.

activities.text: Locals call this maze their “dwaaltuin”—wandering garden. The Doolhof Ruurlo, right next to the castle, was laid out in 1891 on the orders of a Miss Van Heeckeren: 1,188 metres of paths within a hectare of trimmed hedges. Open from April to the end of October. It has a different owner from the museum; expect a separate entrance fee.

practical_info.tip: The maze is open from April 1 to October 31; check on-site hours.

visits.text: The people of Zutphen chained their books in the 16th century for an indisputable reason: theft. The Librije at the Sint Walburgiskerk, built between 1561 and 1564, is the only chained library in the Netherlands still in its original condition. The collection contains around 750 volumes, including first editions of Copernicus and Erasmus. Visits are guided only, throughout the opening day.

Sint Walburgiskerk dates from the 11th century in its oldest parts. It houses a ring-shaped candle chandelier from 1395, a copper holy-water font from 1527 and the Hendrick Bader organ of 1643, restored to its original condition in 1996. The tower can be climbed at weekends and during school holidays, for an unobstructed view over Zutphen and the IJssel. Church entry €10, tower an additional €5.

Looking down over the IJssel from the top of the Walburgiskerk tower is the reward for climbing more than 200 steps. Zutphen, a former Hanseatic city whose golden age stretched from the 13th to the 16th century, retains a compact historic centre with merchant façades fronting buildings that are still inhabited. The Hof van Heeckeren, a 17th-century town palace opposite the Walburgiskerk, houses two museums under one roof.

activities.text: If you appreciate craft beer, the Stadsbrouwerij Cambrinus on the Houtmarkt has brewed its own beers since 2006, in a room with copper brewing vats visible from the tables. The café also offers a selection of Dutch speciality beers. Count on an hour in the evening after sightseeing.

practical_info.tip: Cambrinus is open daily; the vaulted medieval cellar serves as the proeflokaal.

activities.text: Stroll along the Berkelkade beside the River Berkel, which joins the IJssel at Zutphen: Hanseatic warehouses converted into flats and restaurants line the quay. It's the most photographed stretch in town, especially in the evening when the façades are reflected in the water.

practical_info.tip: The Berkelkade is 5 minutes on foot from the Walburgiskerk.

visits.text: Vast, lively and ringed by Renaissance façades, the Brink is astonishing: for a town this size, such architectural coherence is rare in the Netherlands. Museum De Waag occupies a late Gothic building at the centre of the square; archives mention its weighing function as early as the 14th century, and it became a museum in 1915. The terraces come alive from lunchtime onwards, and a market has been held here on Saturday mornings since the Middle Ages.

Deventer's Bergkwartier is one of the best-preserved historic quarters in the Netherlands, with its medieval alleys around the 12th-century Bergkerk. The Muntentoren housed Deventer's last mint until 1708; the Proosdij is one of the oldest stone houses in the Netherlands. In December, the Dickens Festival transforms this quarter into a Victorian stage set with more than 900 costumed characters.

The Dickens Festival in December: unapologetically kitsch, but the 900 costumed characters walking through the streets of the Bergkwartier end up making an impression. Outside the festival, the Grote of Lebuïnuskerk on the edge of the Grote Kerkhof offers a tower climb to 46 meters above the IJssel.

activities.text: Climb the tower of the Grote of Lebuïnuskerk from Grote Kerkhof square: at 46 metres, it overlooks the bend in the IJssel. Deventer is mentioned as early as the 9th century under the name “Daventre”. The view from the tower confirms its strategic position on the river, which explains its medieval power.

practical_info.tip: The tower is accessible on weekends and during school holidays; modest entrance fee.

activities.text: The scent of Deventer Koek has floated over the entire Brink for at least four centuries. This spiced brioche is indeed the town's speciality, sold at the Deventer Koekwinkel on the corner of the square. A bite is a must before leaving. The almond-filled version is the most popular locally.

practical_info.tip: The Deventer Koekwinkel is open daily; a whole cake travels easily.

visits.text: Museum de Fundatie is worth a stop on the way back: its egg-shaped roof—nicknamed “De Wolk”—is clad in 55,000 white-and-blue ceramic tiles from Makkum, added in 2012–2013 to the 19th-century neoclassical building. The collection includes Mondrians and Van Goghs, and temporary exhibitions change constantly.

Stop at Zwolle's Grote Markt square for one last coffee on a terrace before hitting the road. The square is bordered by 15th- and 16th-century merchant façades, with Sint-Michaelskerk closing off the view at the far end. Saturday's market is one of the largest in Overijssel, with several hundred stalls depending on the season.

activities.text: If it's a Wednesday or Saturday, the Sassenpoort is open from 11 am to 5 pm for €3: a quick visit to the Hanseatic hall inside the gate is a fitting way to end the journey exploring the Hanseatic League. From the gate's opening in 1409 to today's return, the Dutch Hanseatic circuit comes full circle.

practical_info.tip: Zwolle station is 15 minutes on foot from the centre; frequent trains to Amsterdam.

seo.h1_title: Eastern Netherlands - Hanseatic League, Veluwe and Achterhoek in 10 Days
seo.intro_paragraph: Ten days through the eastern Netherlands linking Overijssel's Hanseatic towns to the Achterhoek's hidden castles, with the Veluwe and its forest Van Gogh museum in between. A circular route from Zwolle, entirely by car, that skips Amsterdam and shows a side of the country most visitors never see.
seo.seo_hook: From Zwolle's Sassenpoort to Vorden's eight castles: 10 days in the eastern Netherlands exploring the Hanseatic League, Van Gogh in the forest and the medieval Achterhoek.

Giethoorn: car-free village, 180 bridges and 90 km of canals
